q: Define a computer network and list the main network types.
a:
A **computer network** is a collection of computers, servers, mainframes, network devices or other devices connected to one another allowing data to be shared and used.

**Types:** **PAN** (one person, one building) · **LAN** (one building) · **CAN** (group of LANs on the same property) · **MAN** (LANs/CANs in one city) · **WAN** (across a country or countries) · **VPN** (secure connection to a WAN) · **EPN** (one organization connecting its branches) · **SAN** (dedicated network giving servers a shared storage pool).

q: Define network topology and compare bus, ring and star topologies.
a:
**Network topology** is the shape of a LAN, i.e. the ways of connecting computers.

- **Bus:** all devices on one cable with two ends; a single break takes down the entire network; needs **terminators** to stop signal bounce.
- **Ring:** devices in a ring, data flows in the same direction; no ends so **no termination**; a break breaks the circle.
- **Star:** all devices connect to a central control unit; a cable break takes down **one computer**; a central-unit failure takes down the **whole network**.

q: Explain hybrid, mesh, point-to-multipoint and point-to-point topologies.
a:
- **Hybrid:** combines a physical topology with a signaling topology; only two: **star-ring** (ring shrunk in a box) and **star-bus** (bus shrunk in a box).
- **Mesh:** every computer connects to every other; **fully meshed** = direct links, **partially meshed** = via two or more routes.
- **Point-to-multipoint:** one system is the common source; like a star physically but needs an **intelligent central device**.
- **Point-to-point:** two devices connected directly with no central device.

q: Describe the function of: Modem, NIC, Repeater, Hub, Bridge, Switch, Router and WAP.
a:
- **Modem:** dial-up over analog phone lines (internal/external).
- **NIC:** connects a computer to the physical network medium (onboard/card, wired/wireless).
- **Repeater:** solves **attenuation** by regenerating a weak signal.
- **Hub:** **multi-port repeater**, sends the signal to all ports.
- **Bridge:** connects two devices/segments of the same LAN using the same protocol.
- **Switch:** **multi-port bridge**.
- **Router:** connects two or more **different networks**.
- **WAP:** like a hub but connections are through the air.

q: What is a MAC address? Explain its structure with an example.
a:
A **MAC (Media Access Control) address** is a unique **48-bit** identifier burned on a **ROM chip** in the NIC firmware. It is written as **12 hexadecimal characters** (12 × 4 bits = 48 bits = 6 bytes).

Example **E0-69-95-90-8B-C3**: the first six digits (**E0-69-95**) identify the **manufacturer (OUI)**; the last six (**90-8B-C3**) are the NIC's **unique serial number**.

Summarize the history of the Internet.
a:
- **1969:** ARPANET by the U.S. DoD and MIT (after Sputnik).
- **1971:** Ray Tomlinson – first e-mail (SNDMSG, READMAIL).
- **1973–75:** Robert Metcalfe – Alto Aloha network, later **Ethernet**.
- **1974:** Bob Kahn & Vint Cerf – **TCP**.
- **1982–83:** split into MILNET and ARPANET.
- **1984:** **DNS** (Mockapetris, Postel, Partridge).
- **1988:** **IANA** to assign IP numbers.
- **1990:** first ISP World.Std.com.
- **1998:** **ICANN**, coordinates DNS technical elements and manages IANA.

q: Define protocol and port. Compare TCP and UDP.
a:
A **protocol** is a set of rules and instructions for transmitting data between two devices (it defines error checking, compression, how the sender signals the end of a message, and how the receiver signals receipt). A **port** is a location where information is sent through (e.g. HTTP uses port 80).

**TCP:** one-to-one, connection-oriented, segment sequencing, reliable, acknowledgement.
**UDP:** connectionless, no acknowledgement, unreliable, no sequencing.

q: Explain the Internet structure as a network of networks.
a: Subnets (home users, enterprises) connect through a **Point of Presence (PoP)** — e.g. a DSLAM in the telephone central — to a **local ISP**, which connects to a **regional ISP**. Regional ISPs exchange traffic with **global ISPs** at **Internet Exchange Points (IXPs)**. **Content provider networks** (Google, Microsoft) run their own networks to bring content close to users.

q: Compare the types of Internet connection (speed, advantages, disadvantages).
a:
- **Dial-up:** max 56 Kbps; cheap and available; very slow, can't use phone while connected.
- **Cable:** up to 100 Mbps; no phone line; slows at peak, pricier.
- **Fiber (BoF):** 15–150 Mbps; high bandwidth, long distance, EMI resistant; fragile glass, hard to install, signal attenuation/dispersion.
- **DSL/ADSL:** up to 24 Mbps; widespread; must be within ~5 km of the central.
- **VDSL:** 70–100 Mbps; fiber node near the user; depends on copper length.
- **Satellite:** 25–220 Mbps; available anywhere; very expensive, weather-affected, high latency.
- **Mobile:** 4G 3–15 Mbps, 5G 100–1000 Mbps; works while moving; depends on signal and data cost.
